# Insurance Hiring Benchmarks 2026: Time-to-Fill, Cost & Attrition

The structural talent deficit across the U.S. insurance industry is no longer a forward-looking prediction—it is an operational reality. According to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and industry workforce studies, over 50% of the current insurance workforce is over age 45, and more than 100,000 veteran practitioners retire annually. This demographic cliff arrives precisely when carrier balance sheets face compounding pressure from elevated cat loss frequency, inflationary claims costs, and persistent legal system abuse.

For Chief Human Resources Officers, VPs of Talent, and CEOs in property and casualty (P&C), excess & surplus (E&S), life & health (L&H), and insurtech, talent acquisition is no longer an administrative support function. It is a core financial lever. An unfilled commercial underwriting requisition directly translates to unwritten gross written premium (GWP) and unmonitored risk exposure. An understaffed claims department elevates loss adjustment expenses (LAE) and escalates bad-faith litigation risk.

To evaluate where operational performance stands in 2026, talent leaders need hard, sector-specific data. Generic talent benchmarks that pool tech startups, retail, and manufacturing mask the operational frictions unique to insurance. Sourcing a credentialed casualty actuary in Des Moines is fundamentally different from hiring a SaaS account manager in San Francisco.

This report synthesizes real-world talent acquisition performance metrics across the U.S. insurance industry. We examine baseline benchmarks across five key indicators: Time-to-Fill, Cost-per-Hire, Offer Acceptance Rates, Source-of-Hire Mix, and 90-Day Attrition.

---

## Time-to-Fill Breakdown: Actuaries vs. Underwriters vs. Tech

Time-to-fill—measured from the date a requisition receives formal budget approval to the date a candidate formally accepts an offer—varies wildly by role specialization, regulatory complexity, and geographic hub. Across all commercial and personal lines carriers, the industry baseline time-to-fill sits at **62 days**. However, aggregate averages conceal severe operational bottlenecks in technical and revenue-generating desks.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                 TIME-TO-FILL BY ROLE SPECTRUM (DAYS)                  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Personal Lines Claims Adjuster       | [35 - 48 Days]                 |
| Loss Control / Risk Engineer         | [45 - 65 Days]                 |
| Guidewire / Core Systems Engineer    | [55 - 75 Days]                 |
| Commercial P&C Underwriter           | [60 - 85 Days]                 |
| Commercial Sales Producer            | [65 - 90 Days]                 |
| E&S Specialty Underwriter            | [70 - 95 Days]                 |
| Credentialed Actuary (FCAS/FSA)      | [75 - 110 Days]                |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

> **Benchmark:** The national average time-to-fill across all insurance roles sits at 62 days. However, specialized technical roles (FCAS Actuaries, E&S Senior Underwriters) average 88 days, while entry-level claims desks sit at 38 days.

### 1. Actuarial Disciplines (75 – 110 Days)
Credentialed actuaries (Fellows and Associates of the Casualty Actuarial Society or Society of Actuaries) represent the longest hiring cycles in the insurance ecosystem. The talent pool is finite, highly passive, and heavily compensated. Candidates are rarely scanning job boards. Hiring cycles stretch to nearly four months because candidate evaluations routinely involve complex case studies, peer committee panel reviews, and non-compete audits.

### 2. Commercial Underwriting & Specialty Lines (60 – 95 Days)
Commercial P&C underwriters—particularly those handling middle-market, complex commercial, or E&S lines—average 60 to 85 days to fill. In E&S desks where coverage forms are non-standard and technical expertise in niche risks (such as environmental, cyber, or habitational P&C) is non-negotiable, time-to-fill frequently reaches 95 days. Underwriters possess portable books of broker relationships; verifying the strength and compliance of these relationships slows down the offer validation process.

### 3. Claims Operations (35 – 70 Days)
High-volume personal lines auto and property claims adjusters feature the shortest cycles (35 to 48 days), largely driven by structured, continuous interviewing pipelines. Conversely, complex commercial claims examiners—handling complex bodily injury, environmental liability, or construction defect litigation—take between 50 and 70 days. High-volume claims desks carry rapid fill targets, but as detailed later in this report, speed often trades off directly against early candidate retention.

### 4. Insurance Technology & Core Systems (55 – 75 Days)
Engineers with specialized core-system expertise (Guidewire PolicyCenter, ClaimCenter, Duck Creek, or custom insurance data models) take 55 to 75 days to secure. Carriers are competing directly with broad tech firms, while demanding that candidates understand insurance domain logic, state regulatory reporting, and legacy system integrations (such as AS400 core platforms).

### The Real Cost of Bottlenecks: A Hiring Manager's Perspective

> "In early 2025, we left a Senior Commercial Lines Underwriting requisition open in our Charlotte office for 82 days," says Greg Vance, VP of Commercial Lines at a mid-market regional carrier operating across the Southeast. "We thought we were being prudent by holding out for candidate perfection across six interview rounds. 
> 
> By day 60, our existing team was so stretched that our quote turnaround time stretched from 48 hours to 6 days. Local independent agents stopped submitting business to us. We calculated that those extra 30 days of hiring delay cost us over $420,000 in unwritten premium on that single desk. We didn't save money; we lost market share."

---

## Cost-per-Hire and the Real Price of Delayed Requisitions

Standard HR reporting frameworks, including basic SHRM metrics, often cite general corporate cost-per-hire figures between $4,000 and $4,700. In the insurance domain, using aggregate corporate numbers misleads executive leadership. Specialized technical roles, licensed producers, and credentialed underwriters require sophisticated sourcing strategies, industry-specific assessments, and substantial recruitment marketing investments.

Calculated fully—incorporating direct sourcing expenses, external contingency or container fees, recruiter allocations, job board syndication, candidate travel, background checks, state licensing transfer fees, and sign-on guarantees—the true cost-per-hire spans a wide financial continuum.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    COST-PER-HIRE SPECTRUM (USD)                       |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Personal Lines Claims Adjuster       | $4,200 - $7,500                 |
| Risk Engineer / Loss Control         | $8,500 - $15,000                |
| Commercial P&C Underwriter           | $16,000 - $28,000               |
| Core Systems Engineer (Guidewire)    | $18,000 - $32,000               |
| E&S Specialty Underwriter            | $22,000 - $38,000               |
| Commercial Sales Producer            | $25,000 - $55,000               |
| Credentialed Actuary (FCAS/FSA)      | $35,000 - $60,000               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Direct Costs Breakdown

*   **Entry-to-Mid Level Desk Claims Adjusters:** **$4,200 – $7,500**. Sourcing relies on programmatic job advertising, regional campus pipelines, and high-volume digital assessments. Costs remain low, but high turnover forces continuous reinvestment.
*   **Commercial P&C & E&S Underwriters:** **$16,000 – $38,000**. Sourcing requires proactive direct headhunting. When carriers use third-party executive search firms, placement fees run between 20% and 30% of base salary. On a Senior E&S Underwriter earning $140,000 base, agency fees alone sit at $28,000 to $42,000.
*   **Credentialed Actuaries (FCAS/FSA):** **$35,000 – $60,000+**. Due to acute talent scarcity, over 60% of senior actuarial hires involve external search firms, specialized retainers, or heavy sign-on bonuses to offset unvested employer stock or deferred compensation plans.
*   **Commercial Producers:** **$25,000 – $55,000**. Beyond base recruitment costs, producers frequently demand guaranteed commissions or draw periods during their first 12 to 18 months as they transition their target books of business.

### The Hidden Financial Bleed: Unfilled Requisition Costs

To calculate the operational impact of delayed hiring, talent leaders must evaluate the opportunity cost of open desks.

1.  **Underwriting Loss of Production:** A commercial underwriter responsible for an annual GWP book of $6 million yields roughly $16,400 in written premium per calendar day. A 60-day vacancy leaves nearly $1 million in premium writing capacity unserviced or delayed.
2.  **Claims Overtime & Loss Adjustment Expense Inflation:** When claims desks sit vacant, pending case counts spike. To avoid statutory claim-handling violations and bad-faith litigation, carriers reassign claims to existing adjusters or hire third-party independent adjusters (IAs). Independent adjuster fees average $120 to $180 per hour, rapidly multiplying LAE expenses.
3.  **Engineers and Core Systems:** Delays in hiring Guidewire core-system engineers hold up modernization releases. This forces carriers to pay expensive external management consulting rates ($200–$350/hour) to keep digital transformation projects on schedule.

---

## Comprehensive Insurance Talent Benchmarks (2026 Data Matrix)

The matrix below provides talent leaders with an operational baseline across key insurance functions in the U.S. market. Data reflects aggregate operational figures across regional carriers, national personal lines insurers, commercial specialty firms, and insurtech environments.

| Role Category | Time-to-Fill (Days) | Cost-per-Hire ($) | Offer Acceptance Rate (%) | 90-Day Attrition Rate (%) | Primary Sourcing Channel |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Commercial P&C Underwriter (Mid-Senior)** | 60 – 85 | $16,000 – $28,000 | 76% | 11% | Outbound Direct Sourcing / LinkedIn |
| **Specialty / E&S Underwriter** | 70 – 95 | $22,000 – $38,000 | 71% | 8% | Specialized Headhunting / Niche Networks |
| **Actuary (Credentialed FCAS/FSA)** | 75 – 110 | $35,000 – $60,000 | 68% | 6% | Target Executive Search / Employee Referral |
| **Personal Lines Claims Adjuster** | 35 – 48 | $4,200 – $7,500 | 84% | 22% | High-Volume Sourcing / Job Boards |
| **Complex / Commercial Claims Examiner** | 50 – 70 | $10,000 – $18,000 | 78% | 12% | Targeted Outbound / Employee Referral |
| **Core Systems Engineer (Guidewire/Duck Creek)**| 55 – 75 | $18,000 – $32,000 | 72% | 14% | Tech Headhunting / Specialized Agencies |
| **Commercial Producer / Broker** | 65 – 90 | $25,000 – $55,000 | 65% | 18% | Professional Networks / Executive Search |
| **Risk Engineer / Loss Control Specialist** | 45 – 65 | $8,500 – $15,000 | 80% | 9% | Trade Associations / Direct Sourcing |

### Key Takeaways from the Data Matrix

*   **Inverse Relationship Between Cost and Attrition:** Roles with high initial recruitment costs (Actuaries, E&S Underwriters) maintain low 90-day attrition (6%–8%). Conversely, low cost-per-hire roles (Personal Lines Adjusters) feature high early turnover (22%), indicating that low initial candidate acquisition expenditure often leads to higher downstream replacement costs.
*   **Offer Acceptance Suppression in Sales and Specialty Roles:** Commercial Producers (65%) and Actuaries (68%) exhibit the lowest offer acceptance rates. Producers hesitate due to restrictive covenants, non-solicit legal risks, and unpromising book transfers. Actuaries drop out due to aggressive retention counter-offers from incumbent employers.

---

## Offer Acceptance Rates: Winning Candidates in a Risk-Averse Market

Across all professional sectors, insurance professionals display higher-than-average risk aversion. Given that risk management is their primary professional discipline, candidates evaluate potential career moves through a meticulous risk-reward framework.

In 2026, the aggregate national offer acceptance rate for insurance roles sits at **76%**. However, when analyzing candidates in high demand—such as senior actuaries, Guidewire developers, and commercial underwriters with established agency relationships—acceptance rates sink below **70%**.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    OFFER ACCEPTANCE RATES BY ROLE                     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Personal Lines Claims Adjuster       | [====================] 84%     |
| Risk Engineer / Loss Control         | [=================== ] 80%     |
| Complex / Commercial Claims Examiner | [==================  ] 78%     |
| Commercial P&C Underwriter           | [==================  ] 76%     |
| Core Systems Engineer (Guidewire)    | [=================   ] 72%     |
| E&S Specialty Underwriter            | [=================   ] 71%     |
| Credentialed Actuary (FCAS/FSA)      | [================    ] 68%     |
| Commercial Sales Producer            | [===============     ] 65%     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Primary Friction Points Causing Candidate Drop-Off

#### 1. Work Arrangement Ambiguity & RTO Mandates
Strict Return-to-Office (RTO) policies create major hiring friction. Carriers enforcing 4- or 5-day mandatory office presence in regional hubs like Hartford, CT, or Des Moines, IA, suffer offer acceptance rates **15 to 20 percentage points lower** than carriers offering flexible hybrid models (1–2 days in office) or remote arrangements. Experienced commercial underwriters frequently reject offers if forced back into rigid daily commutes.

#### 2. Protracted Approval Processes and Counter-Offers
High-performing insurance professionals are rarely unemployed. When interview processes extend past three rounds or suffer delays from multi-layered compensation committees, current employers have time to craft aggressive counter-offers. Over 40% of declined offers in underwriting and actuarial fields stem directly from incumbent counter-offers matched with unexpected salary bumps or remote work concessions.

#### 3. Financial Ratings and Capacity Concerns
Candidates evaluate carrier stability. Underwriters are reluctant to join carriers that have recently suffered A.M. Best downgrades or are aggressively shrinking capacity in key operating territories (such as personal property in Florida or commercial liability in California). Candidates know that limited underwriting capacity makes hitting production bonuses nearly impossible.

### Field Insight: Eliminating Decision Bottlenecks

> "We were losing one out of every three underwriting candidates at the offer stage," explains Sarah Jenkins, VP of Talent Acquisition at a mid-market carrier in Des Moines. "Our hiring managers were taking 10 business days to route formal offer letters through three executive sign-offs. 
> 
> By the time the offer landed, the candidate had either accepted a counter-offer or signed with a faster competitor. We restructured our authority matrix, gave HR sign-off capability within clear salary bands, and cut offer turnaround time down to 24 hours post-interview. Our offer acceptance rate immediately surged from 66% to 82%."

---

## Source-of-Hire Mix: The Fall of Inbound Job Boards and the Rise of Direct Sourcing

Inbound application channels (including corporate career sites, Indeed, and general LinkedIn postings) yield lower return on investment than ever before. While application volume has surged by more than 300% due to generative AI resume tools, candidate quality has plummeted. Talent acquisition leaders report that **less than 5% of inbound applicants** for specialized underwriting, actuarial, or complex claims roles meet minimum qualification benchmarks.

To build predictable talent pipelines, carriers have shifted away from transactional job postings toward outbound sourcing, internal referral networks, and specialized recruiting partnerships.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    SOURCE-OF-HIRE BREAKDOWN (2026)                    |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Outbound Direct Sourcing             | [==================  ] 40%     |
| Employee Referrals                   | [==============      ] 30%     |
| Specialized Recruitment Partners     | [======              ] 15%     |
| Inbound Job Boards                   | [====                ] 10%     |
| Internal Mobility & Apprenticeships  | [==                  ] 5%      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Strategic Channel Analysis

#### 1. Direct Sourcing & Talent Mapping (40% of Successful Hires)
Top-performing insurance talent teams operate proactive sourcing engines. Sourcing teams map competitors across specific lines of business and regions—identifying Commercial P&C Underwriters at national carriers and reaching out with targeted value propositions. Using platforms like LinkedIn Recruiter alongside specialized talent market tools, direct outbound recruitment generates the highest-quality candidate slates.

#### 2. Employee Referral Programs (30% of Successful Hires)
Insurance is a tightly connected industry network. Referral programs deliver high candidate match rates and exceptional 90-day retention. Leading carriers offer tiered referral bonuses: $2,500 for entry-to-mid roles, scaling up to $7,500–$10,000 for hard-to-fill credentialed actuaries, specialty underwriters, and sales producers.

#### 3. Specialized Recruitment Partners (15% of Successful Hires)
For critical niche vacancies—such as E&S Directors, Chief Actuaries, or Guidewire Transformation Leaders—carriers rely on specialized external partners. These partners maintain passive talent networks that do not register on standard job boards or public search databases.

#### 4. Inbound Job Boards (10% of Successful Hires)
Inbound portals now serve primarily as secondary validation tools or mechanisms for entry-level claims and customer service roles. Relying on inbound job boards for technical or revenue-generating insurance desks creates administrative overload for talent teams without producing viable shortlists.

#### 5. Internal Mobility & Apprenticeships (5% of Successful Hires)
Faced with talent shortages, carriers are expanding internal upskilling programs. Claims adjusters with strong analytical skills are trained for underwriting desks, while customer service agents transition into entry-level claims handling. Additionally, modern apprenticeship programs—co-developed with universities in regional hubs like Charlotte and Columbus—are showing strong long-term retention returns.

---

## The 90-Day Attrition Crisis: Why Early Flight Risk Is Killing Insurance Margins

Securing candidate offer acceptances is only half the battle. The first 90 days of employment represent a major structural vulnerability for carriers. The average 90-day voluntary and involuntary attrition rate across the U.S. insurance industry sits at **14%**, but surges to **22%** in high-volume personal lines claims environments.

Early turnover is exceptionally costly. It wipes out recruitment investments, disrupts team morale, overburdens remaining employees, and risks customer and agent relationship damage.

> **Benchmark:** The average cost of 90-day attrition for a commercial underwriting or senior claims role exceeds $45,000 when accounting for lost productivity, unrecovered sign-on bonuses, repeat recruiter fees, and re-interview overhead.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    90-DAY ATTRITION RATES BY DESK                     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Personal Lines Claims Adjuster       | [====================] 22%     |
| Commercial Sales Producer            | [=================   ] 18%     |
| Core Systems Engineer (Guidewire)    | [==============      ] 14%     |
| Complex / Commercial Claims Examiner | [============        ] 12%     |
| Commercial P&C Underwriter           | [===========         ] 11%     |
| Risk Engineer / Loss Control         | [=========           ] 9%      |
| Specialty / E&S Underwriter          | [========            ] 8%      |
| Credentialed Actuary (FCAS/FSA)      | [======              ] 6%      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Core Causes of 90-Day Attrition in Insurance

#### 1. Tech Stack Disconnect and Operational Friction
During interviews, carriers highlight digital transformation plans. In practice, new hires often land in legacy environments powered by mainframe applications, manual spreadsheet workarounds, and fragmented document management systems. For underwriters and claims adjusters accustomed to modern workflows, dealing with severe operational friction causes immediate frustration.

#### 2. Heavy File Workloads and Production Targets
In claims desks, new hires are often hit with unmanageable pending file volumes during their first 30 days. When adjusters inherit hundreds of messy pending files without proper onboarding support, burn-out triggers early resignations.

#### 3. Mismatched Authority Limits and Product Autonomy
Newly hired underwriters often discover that their promised underwriting authority is constrained by rigid corporate referral triggers. When underwriters must pass basic middle-market risk decisions up through complex regional referral chains, they feel micro-managed and restricted in their ability to build relationships with independent agents.

#### 4. Disjointed Remote & Hybrid Onboarding
As carriers moved to hybrid work models, many failed to modernize their training frameworks. Bringing on a remote or hybrid underwriter requires structured shadowing, deliberate carrier risk-appetite training, and formal mentor pairings. Without structured touchpoints, new hires feel isolated and disengaged.

---

## Regional Talent Hotspots & Geographic Arbitrage in 2026

Insurance hiring in the U.S. has broken out of its traditional geographic concentrations. While traditional operational centers like **Hartford, CT** and **Des Moines, IA** remain vital, significant talent shifts have expanded the geographic operational landscape.

Carriers actively leverage geographic talent strategy—establishing satellite operations, hub offices, or remote clusters in cost-competitive, candidate-dense metropolitan regions across the Sunbelt and Midwest.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     U.S. INSURANCE TALENT HUBS                        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  TRADITIONAL HUBS                   EMERGING MICRO-HUBS               |
|  * Hartford, CT                     * Charlotte, NC                   |
|  * Des Moines, IA                   * Atlanta, GA                     |
|  * Chicago, IL                      * Salt Lake City, UT              |
|  * New York / New Jersey Metro      * Columbus, OH                    |
|                                     * Austin, TX                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Key Regional Micro-Hubs Analysis

#### Charlotte, North Carolina
*   **Talent Specialization:** Commercial P&C Underwriting, Financial Lines, Excess & Surplus, Reinsurance.
*   **Operational Dynamics:** Charlotte has expanded beyond banking into a powerhouse for commercial insurance talent across the Southeast. Mid-market carriers and brokers benefit from a strong talent pool, favorable business climate, and accessible executive talent. Underwriter compensation levels track roughly 8% below New York/Boston metros, offering cost-efficiency alongside deep domain expertise.

#### Atlanta, Georgia
*   **Talent Specialization:** Complex Claims Operations, E&S Surplus Lines, Commercial Liability, Wholesale Brokerage.
*   **Operational Dynamics:** Atlanta serves as a dominant center for E&S wholesale brokers, managing general agents (MGAs), and regional claims handling operations. The market features strong expertise in complex commercial auto, trucking, and general liability, though competition for experienced claims examiners remains high.

#### Salt Lake City, Utah
*   **Talent Specialization:** Insurtech Engineering, Customer Experience, Regional Personal Lines Claims, Digital Product Management.
*   **Operational Dynamics:** Salt Lake City provides an attractive balance of tech engineering talent and operational capabilities. Carriers use the region to build out modern core platform development hubs and regional claims operations—benefiting from a younger demographic profile and strong university pipelines.

#### Columbus, Ohio
*   **Talent Specialization:** Personal & Commercial Lines Operations, Actuarial Analytics, Risk Data Engineering, Carrier Back-Office.
*   **Operational Dynamics:** Home to major carrier headquarters, Columbus boasts high concentrations of insurance talent per capita. It features a deep market for data analysts, product managers, and underwriting support teams. Salary levels remain highly competitive relative to coastal benchmarks.

#### Austin, Texas
*   **Talent Specialization:** Insurtech Innovation, Predictive Modeling, Automated Claims Engineering, Direct-to-Consumer Distribution.
*   **Operational Dynamics:** Austin remains a focal point for carriers building modern digital transformation hubs. While compensation matches tech-sector pay scales, the concentration of full-stack engineers and machine learning talent makes it a prime location for digital core transformations.

### Managing Salary Arbitrage Across Regions

With geographic dispersion comes salary variance. While executive roles (Chief Actuary, Head of Underwriting) command fully nationalized compensation scales regardless of location, mid-level roles display clear regional band differentials:

*   **Hartford / NY Metro:** 110% – 120% of national baseline compensation.
*   **Charlotte / Atlanta / Austin:** 98% – 105% of national baseline compensation.
*   **Des Moines / Columbus / Salt Lake City:** 90% – 96% of national baseline compensation.

Carriers that implement dynamic regional pay bands maintain clear cost-per-hire advantages while expanding access to candidate pools outside traditional legacy hubs.

## Action Plan for Insurance Talent Leaders

To improve operational talent performance in 2026, talent leaders must modernize their recruiting models to match industry realities. Achieving sustainable recruitment performance requires focused, structural execution across four key operational areas:

### 1. Compress Interview Loops to Protect Acceptance Rates
*   **Action:** Audit interview steps across every desk. Eliminate redundant interview rounds. Limit professional candidate evaluations to a maximum of **three stages** completed within a 14-day window.
*   **Target:** Reduce Time-to-Fill by 15–20 days and increase Offer Acceptance Rates above 80%.

### 2. Shift Investments from Passive Job Boards to Outbound Sourcing
*   **Action:** Reallocate recruitment advertising budgets away from general job aggregators toward proactive outbound direct sourcing, specialized industry databases, and employee referral incentives.
*   **Target:** Increase outbound direct-hire contributions to more than 40% of total hires while cutting agency reliance.

### 3. Formalize Onboarding to Guard Against 90-Day Attrition
*   **Action:** Build dedicated 90-day onboarding programs that combine system training, structured peer mentoring, transparent workload ramp-up schedules, and 30-/60-/90-day check-ins.
*   **Target:** Keep early claims attrition under 12% and underwriting/actuarial 90-day attrition under 5%.

### 4. Optimize Geographic Sourcing for High-Demand Roles
*   **Action:** Establish regional hiring hubs in candidate-dense markets like Charlotte, Columbus, Atlanta, and Salt Lake City to access deeper candidate pools and manage compensation inflation.
*   **Target:** Reduce cost-per-hire by 10–15% while building geographic talent redundancy.
